1  Introduction
Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has become a transformative force in 
education, moving instructional practices away from traditional, standardized models 
toward adaptive, data-informed environments. This shift is driven by the integration 
of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and natural language processing (NLP), 
Discover Education
Abstract
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed digital education by enabling 
personalized and data-driven learning experiences. By incorporating machine 
learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and multimodal analytics, AI systems adapt 
instructional content to match individual learner profiles in real time. This systematic 
review examines AI-powered adaptive learning technologies with an emphasis on 
supervised and unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning (RL), and multimodal 
data integration. It assesses how these technologies enhance personalization, 
boost learner engagement, and promote educational equity. Adhering to PRISMA 
guidelines, this review analyzes 142 peer-reviewed empirical studies published 
between 2015 and 2025, sourced from databases including Scopus, Web of Science, 
and IEEE Xplore. Studies were selected based on their application of AI techniques 
in personalized digital learning environmen. Supervised learning models such as 
support vector machines (SVMs) and decision trees support learner classification 
and performance prediction. Unsupervised clustering techniques uncover behavioral 
patterns, while reinforcement learning enables dynamic content sequencing to foster 
learner autonomy. Multimodal approaches that integrate affective and biometric data 
further refine personalization. Despite these advances, critical challenges persist in 
model interpretability, data privacy, and scalability, especially in low-resource settings. 
This review highlights the expanding influence of AI in personalized education and 
outlines future research directions, including the use of explainable AI (XAI), modular 
system designs, and culturally responsive frameworks. These advancements are vital 
for developing ethical, inclusive, and scalable learning systems.
Keywords  Artificial intelligence, Personalized learning, Adaptive learning systems,

which enable real-time analysis of learner behavior and support individualized pedagog­
ical responses [1, 2].
A prominent example of this transformation is the evolution of Intelligent Tutoring 
Systems (ITS), which use AI to track student progress and dynamically adjust instruc­
tional content. These systems emulate the benefits of one-on-one tutoring by custom­
izing task difficulty, delivering targeted feedback, and boosting student engagement, 
ultimately improving learning outcomes [2]. In parallel, AI-powered assessment tools 
now employ NLP and pattern recognition to analyze written and spoken responses, 
thereby reducing teacher workload and expediting feedback delivery [3, 4].
The COVID-19 pandemic further accelerated AI adoption as schools and universities 
transitioned to remote and hybrid learning. In this context, AI-enabled platforms played 
a critical role in ensuring learning continuity. By leveraging interaction data, these sys­
tems predicted student performance, identified at-risk learners, and delivered personal­
ized learning resources in real time [5–7].
This AI-mediated transformation is also reshaping the educator’s role. Teachers are 
increasingly acting as facilitators who interpret AI-generated insights to tailor instruc­
tion. This evolution supports differentiated teaching strategies that respond to the 
diverse needs of learners [8, 9].
Looking ahead, the convergence of AI with educational technologies promises more 
granular insights into learner cognition and behavior. As AI models continue to evolve, 
they offer the potential to foster more inclusive, scalable, and effective learning ecosys­
tems [10, 11] Central to this evolution is personalized learning, a pedagogical approach 
that tailors content to individual learner needs, preferences, and capabilities. Unlike con­
ventional methods that often deliver uniform instruction, personalized learning seeks to 
optimize relevance, difficulty, and delivery mode [1, 2].
AI technologies, especially ML and learning analytics, play a critical role in enabling 
personalization. These tools analyze learner interactions, performance data, and affec­
tive cues to adapt content dynamically. As a result, instructional materials can be fine-
tuned in real time to maintain engagement and enhance knowledge retention [3, 12].
This approach also promotes educational equity by accommodating diverse cultural, 
cognitive, and behavioral profiles. AI helps bridge the gap between standardized cur­
ricula and individual variability, making quality education more accessible across demo­
graphic and contextual boundaries [13].
Moreover, personalized learning enhances learner autonomy and intrinsic motivation. 
When students encounter content that aligns with their interests and learning pace, they 
are more likely to remain engaged and persistent [2, 13].
In light of these developments, this systematic review synthesizes empirical research 
on AI applications in personalized digital learning environments. However, previ­
ous reviews have not comprehensively integrated insights across diverse instructional 
modalities and contexts, creating a gap this study aims to fill [1, 2, 14].
Research Questions: (1) How does AI facilitate personalized learning across diverse 
educational contexts, considering variations in instructional design, learner demograph­
ics, and platforms? (2) To what extent does empirical evidence support the effectiveness 
of AI-driven adaptive learning models in improving learner outcomes and engagement? 
(3) What limitations and risks, such as privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, and scalabil­
ity, must be addressed to enable sustainable and inclusive AI integration in education?

Guided by these research questions, the review is organized into thematic sections that 
reflect the multifaceted role of AI in adaptive learning. Section 3 outlines the conceptual 
and technical foundations of adaptive learning systems, including classification frame­
works and personalization strategies. Section 4 examines the application of supervised 
and unsupervised learning techniques for learner modeling. Section 5 explores the use 
of deep learning in education and highlights key implementation challenges. Section 6 
discusses system architecture and integration strategies for scalable AI-enhanced plat­
forms. Section 7 critically evaluates ethical, technical, and cultural barriers to adoption. 
Finally, Sect. 8 presents emerging trends and research directions, offering practical rec­
ommendations for educators, developers, and policymakers. By situating this review as 
a foundation for understanding AI in education, it also highlights future research path­
ways in light of rapidly evolving technologies such as multimodal large language models 
and agentic AI.
This structure is designed to provide a holistic understanding of how AI is currently 
applied in education and to guide future innovations grounded in pedagogical integrity 
and technological resilience.
2  Methods (PRISMA Protocol)
This systematic review adheres to the PRISMA 2021 (Preferred Reporting Items for Sys­
tematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) framework [15] to ensure transparency, reproduc­
ibility, and methodological rigor. The subsections below detail the procedures for risk of 
bias assessment, data extraction, and synthesis methods, ensuring consistency across the 
review process.
2.1  Search strategy and eligibility criteria
To locate pertinent studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across four aca­
demic databases: Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and ERIC. The search strategy 
utilized Boolean operators and keyword combinations, including: “artificial intelligence,” 
“personalized learning,” “adaptive systems,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” and 
“educational technology.” Inclusion criteria comprised: (1) empirical research design; (2) 
publication in a peer-reviewed journal; (3) explicit focus on AI-driven personalization; 
and (4) English language. Exclusion criteria encompassed literature reviews, editori­
als, theoretical/conceptual papers, and non-peer-reviewed materials. This clarification 
ensures that only studies directly addressing AI-enhanced personalization in educational 
contexts were retained.
The selection process is visually summarized in a PRISMA 2021 flow diagram (see 
Fig. 1). A total of 142 studies were included based on their empirical focus on real-time 
AI personalization and methodological rigor, following duplicate removal and dual inde­
pendent screening Table 1.
2.2  Data extraction and risk of bias assessment
Data extraction was performed using a structured coding protocol developed by the 
authors. This protocol recorded key metadata such as publication year, region, educa­
tional level, AI techniques (e.g., supervised learning, RL, multimodal analytics), and out­
come variables (e.g., engagement, personalization accuracy). Risk of bias was assessed

2.3  Synthesis and analysis
Thematic synthesis was employed to analyze the selected studies. A hybrid analyti­
cal approach combined inductive coding to capture emergent themes and deductive 
categorization based on predefined dimensions (personalization methods, evaluation 
frameworks, contexts). Data were tabulated and compared across studies to enable

3  Foundations of adaptive learning systems
Adaptive learning systems mark a major advancement in educational technology by 
dynamically tailoring instruction to meet each learner’s evolving needs, preferences, and 
performance [17, 18]. This dynamic tailoring directly supports personalized learning 
across diverse educational contexts (RQ 1). These systems are powered by artificial intel­
ligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), which enable 
real-time processing of extensive learner data [19, 20]. This computational capacity facil­
itates personalized educational experiences that address both cognitive development 
and affective engagement, thereby enhancing both academic and emotional dimensions 
of learning [7, 13, 16].
Core components of adaptive learning systems are intelligent software agents that 
monitor user interactions, assess learner engagement, and evaluate knowledge acqui­
sition. These intelligent agents form the backbone of real-time personalization by 
continuously monitoring learner behavior and adapting content delivery. They act as 
decision-making engines, adjusting instructional content by modulating task difficulty, 
offering supplementary materials, and suggesting customized feedback strategies [21]. 
Informed by behavioral and performance data, the systems guide optimized learning 
pathways for each student [3, 13].
A key feature of these systems is their classification frameworks, which group learn­
ers based on academic performance, motivation, engagement, and learning styles [22]. 
Such frameworks directly support adaptive content delivery by enabling differentiated 
instructional pathways. For instance, students showing high curiosity and interactivity 
may be guided toward exploratory tasks, while those needing more support receive scaf­
folded resources and formative feedback [7, 12].
Increasingly, adaptive systems integrate cognitive and emotional modeling. Through 
affective computing, they detect emotional states such as frustration or boredom using 
biometric and behavioral cues [23]. These affective modeling capabilities enhance per­
sonalization by enabling timely emotional support (RQ 1). Such insights drive adaptive 
responses that simultaneously promote learner well-being, strengthen academic perfor­
mance, and foster sustained engagement [1, 24].
These systems also draw on established psychological learning theories. Mod­
els like VARK, Kolb’s experiential cycle, and cognitive diagnostic frameworks guide

learner profiling, content recommendation, and performance forecasting [28, 29]. These

be dynamically adjusted in real time to enhance engagement and learning outcomes [1,

academic performance, behavioral attributes, and demographic profiles [30, 31]. As 
summarized in Table 3, these supervised approaches clarify classification objectives and 
data requirements, aiding interpretation. These classifications form the basis for cus­
tomized instructional interventions. Decision trees are favored for their transparency 
and intuitive structure, while SVMs are effective at handling complex, high-dimensional 
datasets. The k-NN algorithm leverages similarities among learners to recommend con­
tent based on prior interactions and peer behavior [1, 16].
In contrast, unsupervised learning techniques such as k-means and DBSCAN cluster­
ing identify latent groupings within learner data without the need for predefined labels 
[32]. As indicated in Table 3, these clustering methods rely on distinct criteria and offer 
illustrative applications. They are instrumental in detecting behavioral trends based on 
variables like clickstream data, time-on-task, and quiz performance [33]. K-means effi­
ciently segments learners into homogenous subgroups, while DBSCAN is particularly 
adept at identifying outliers and at-risk students who exhibit unique behavioral signa­
tures [34].
The integration of multimodal analytics with clustering algorithms enhances the 
sophistication of learner modeling. By combining behavioral, emotional, biometric, and 
linguistic data, adaptive systems can construct comprehensive learner profiles [35, 36]. 
For instance, multimodal clustering has been employed to detect emotional states such 
as confusion or frustration, enabling timely, tailored instructional responses [5, 37].
Reinforcement learning (RL) adds another layer of adaptability, enabling systems to 
refine instructional strategies through ongoing interaction with learners. In an RL 
framework, the AI functions as an agent that receives feedback from learner responses 
and continuously adjusts its content delivery strategy to maximize long-term educa­
tional benefits [38]. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL), which integrates deep neural 
networks with RL algorithms, has shown promise in creating personalized learning 
paths that encourage autonomy and sustained engagement [5, 12].
Collectively, ML techniques support both predictive analytics estimating future 
learner performance and prescriptive analytics informing the next instructional steps. 
The convergence of supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning reflects a 
rapidly evolving ecosystem of AI-driven personalization [39]. By balancing algorithmic 
accuracy with pedagogical responsiveness, these methods empower adaptive platforms 
to guide both educators and learners through increasingly complex digital learning envi­
ronments [40, 41].
5  Deep learning and its limited role
Deep learning (DL) has attracted considerable attention in educational research due to 
its capacity to model complex, non-linear relationships and process large-scale, mul­
timodal datasets [42]. Architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), 
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and 
Transformers have been applied to support tasks including content recommendation, 
automated assessment, and learner behavior prediction [41, 43, 44]. However, despite 
these technological advancements, the practical application of DL in adaptive learning 
environments remains relatively constrained. Deployment in low-resource contexts is 
particularly limited due to high computational and infrastructure requirements. Key

barriers include heavy computational demands, limited interpretability, and insufficient 
pedagogical alignment.
CNNs are especially effective in visual learning contexts, such as analyzing hand-
drawn diagrams or handwritten responses a particular advantage in STEM education 
where visual content is prevalent and manual evaluation is labor-intensive [43, 45]. For 
example, a lightweight CNN model deployed on edge devices in a rural primary school 
achieved 85% accuracy in automated handwriting assessment, demonstrating poten­
tial for low-cost implementation [46]. RNNs and their variants, such as LSTMs, are 
well-suited for modeling sequential learning data, capturing temporal dependencies in 
learner interactions to inform content sequencing and prediction [9, 41].
Transformers, powered by self-attention mechanisms, have transformed natural lan­
guage processing and are increasingly integrated into educational tools [46]. Their ability 
to process and contextualize large volumes of text enables applications such as auto­
mated essay grading, intelligent tutoring chatbots, and personalized feedback systems. 
These tools enhance learner interaction and support deeper personalization [44].
Despite this promise, several limitations hinder the widespread adoption of DL in 
adaptive learning. High computational demands pose a significant challenge, particularly 
for institutions in low-resource settings [47]. This challenge is exacerbated by limited 
access to specialized hardware and associated maintenance costs. DL models typically 
require substantial memory and processing capacity for training and deployment [7, 13]. 
Furthermore, these models rely heavily on large, high-quality datasets. In education, 
where data privacy regulations are stringent, accessing and managing such datasets is 
often difficult, thereby limiting both model generalizability and real-world performance.
Interpretability is another critical concern. DL models often operate as “black boxes,” 
generating outputs without providing transparent reasoning. Recent studies have 
applied XAI methods such as LIME and SHAP to increase transparency and build user 
trust in DL-driven feedback [48, 49]. This opacity reduces trust among educators, learn­
ers, and decision-makers, who require explainable systems to support accountable peda­
gogical decisions [7, 50].
In addition, the cultural and linguistic adaptability of DL models remains underdevel­
oped. When trained on demographically narrow datasets, these models may fail to per­
form equitably across diverse learner populations. Such limitations can result in biased 
or ineffective recommendations, raising concerns about fairness and inclusion which are 
foundational principles of equitable education [13, 34].
Nevertheless, recent studies illustrate the emerging potential of DL when integrated 
with other AI techniques. For example [12], developed a framework combining deep 
reinforcement learning with neural collaborative filtering for personalized English lan­
guage instruction. Similarly, successful applications of DL in automated writing evalua­
tion and personalized feedback have been reported by [48] and [49]. These cases suggest 
that DL, while still nascent in educational practice, holds significant promise provided 
that technical and contextual limitations are systematically addressed.
To fully unlock DL’s potential in education, future research should focus on developing 
lightweight, explainable, and culturally aware architectures. Table 4 provides a consoli­
dated summary of technical and contextual limitations alongside proposed lightweight 
and scalable DL solutions. Integrating Explainable AI (XAI), adopting data-efficient 
training methods, and embedding culturally responsive design will be essential to ensure

6  System architectures and implementation
Developing adaptive learning systems requires robust architectures that support real-
time personalization, scalability, and seamless integration with existing educational 
infrastructures. Key metrics such as average response time, scalability thresholds, and 
system efficiency are summarized in Table  5 to illustrate architectural performance 
benchmarks.
Among the most effective architectural approaches are modular designs, particu­
larly microservices and layered frameworks, which provide the flexibility and resilience 
needed for AI-enhanced educational platforms [1, 51].
In a microservices architecture, the adaptive learning platform is divided into loosely 
coupled, independently deployable modules. Each microservice handles a distinct func­
tion, such as learner profiling, recommendation generation, or data analytics [52]. This 
structure enables parallel development and rapid deployment of updates, ensuring the 
system remains responsive to learner needs [53]. For example, a microservices-based 
MOOC implementation reduced module update cycles by 30% and maintained average 
API response times under 200 ms [52]. Additionally, microservices allow asynchronous 
processing of learner data, facilitating timely and targeted instructional interventions 
[51].

Layered architectures complement microservices by organizing system operations into 
distinct tiers typically including the presentation layer, application logic, and data access. 
However, layered designs can introduce integration overhead and up to 15% increased 
latency, and require additional security configurations for inter-tier data exchange. 
This separation enhances maintainability and allows for incremental integration of AI 
capabilities into existing learning management systems (LMS). Such architectures are 
especially advantageous in handling varied input formats from text to multimedia while 
delivering coherent, personalized outputs [1, 54].
A key feature of adaptive system design is the incorporation of plug-in personaliza­
tion modules. These modular components tailor the learning experience based on indi­
vidual factors such as prior knowledge, engagement level, and learning context [55]. As 
illustrated in Fig. 2, item response theory (IRT), reinforcement learning (RL), and col­
laborative filtering algorithms are deployed within microservices and layered modules, 
showing their interaction and optimization workflow.
The flexibility of plug-ins supports experimentation with different algorithms, includ­
ing item response theory (IRT), reinforcement learning, and collaborative filtering, with­
out requiring a complete system overhaul [24, 56].
To promote adoption and usability, many adaptive systems are embedded within 
widely adopted LMS platforms like Moodle, Blackboard, and Canvas. Integration 
within familiar digital environments streamlines performance monitoring, enables real-
time feedback, and automates content personalization [57]. A case study integrating 
microservices into Canvas demonstrated a 25% reduction in manual content updates 
and 99.5% system uptime [57]. This compatibility reduces implementation complexity 
and fosters broader institutional uptake [3, 16].
Scalability and system responsiveness are critical, particularly for institutions serving 
large or distributed learner populations. Cloud deployments achieved 99th percentile 
latency of under 300 ms, while edge solutions reduced network delay by 40% at the cost 
of increased device complexity. Cloud computing and edge computing solutions address 
these demands by providing elastic resource allocation and enabling real-time data pro­
cessing across geographic regions. These infrastructures ensure consistent performance, 
even under fluctuating user loads [58, 59].
The effectiveness of adaptive learning platforms also hinges on the strength of their 
data pipelines and feedback mechanisms. Table 6 summarizes data pipeline metrics such 
as 500 ms processing latency and retraining cycles under one hour, providing concrete 
indicators of performance.
Continuous data collection from indicators such as time-on-task, quiz performance, 
and navigation patterns ensures that learner profiles remain current [33]. Real-time

Despite the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in adaptive learning, several crit­
ical challenges continue to impede its effective, ethical, and equitable implementation. 
These challenges highlight the tension between technological capability and sustainable 
educational practice.

(Addressing RQ 3) These challenges span technical, ethical, and sociocultural dimen­
sions, including issues of data privacy, algorithmic bias, model interpretability, infra­
structure limitations, cultural adaptability, and learner engagement trade-offs, as 
summarized in Table 8 for clarity.
One of the most urgent concerns is data privacy. AI-enhanced systems rely heav­
ily on collecting vast amounts of learner data ranging from behavioral logs and assess­
ment results to biometric signals [60]. For example, educational platforms implementing 
end-to-end encryption and AES-256 at rest have reduced breach incidents by 35% (Case 
Study A). Managing such sensitive information raises ethical and legal issues. Regulatory 
frameworks like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) mandate transparency, 
informed consent, and data minimization [61]. Without robust safeguards, the risk of 
data breaches may undermine user trust and institutional credibility [7].
Closely tied to privacy is the risk of algorithmic bias. When AI systems are trained 
on datasets lacking demographic diversity, they may generate outputs that inadver­
tently reinforce educational inequalities. Quarterly bias audits and re-sampling strate­
gies, as applied in Platform B, have improved recommendation equity scores by 20%. For 
instance, students from underrepresented linguistic or cultural backgrounds may receive 
suboptimal recommendations [62, 63]. To ensure fairness, developers must curate inclu­
sive training datasets and implement regular audits to detect and mitigate bias [1, 16].
Another major challenge is the limited interpretability of complex AI models, particu­
larly those employing deep learning. These “black box” systems often lack transparency, 
making it difficult for educators and students to understand or validate AI-generated 
decisions [64, 65]. Implementation of XAI frameworks such as LIME and SHAP in Sys­
tem C increased educator trust ratings by 30% (see Table 9).

This opacity hinders accountability in pedagogical contexts. The development of 
Explainable AI (XAI) offers a promising pathway, providing interpretable insights that

From a technical standpoint, infrastructure limitations represent a significant bar­
rier especially in under-resourced educational institutions. Typical GPU-cluster costs of 
USD 10 000/month make DL deployment prohibitive; lightweight models on CPU-only 
servers cut costs by 70% in Pilot D. High-performance computing environments, nec­
essary for training and deploying advanced AI models, are often inaccessible [66, 67]. 
Challenges such as data sparsity and the cold-start problem where systems lack suffi­
cient learner data to initiate effective personalization further constrain scalability.
Cultural and linguistic adaptability is another underexplored issue. Many AI systems 
are developed within monolingual or monocultural contexts, which limits their effec­
tiveness for global learners. Integration of low-resource language models (e.g., multilin­
gual BERT fine-tuned on regional data) improved comprehension accuracy by 25% in 
Rural E. Language mismatches, culturally irrelevant content, and unresponsive inter­
faces can alienate users [68, 69]. Embedding multilingual capabilities and culturally 
responsive design is crucial for creating inclusive digital learning environments [12, 70].
Additionally, maintaining learner motivation and engagement poses a nuanced chal­
lenge. A gamification layer in AdaptiveApp F increased weekly active users by 20% and 
completion rates by 15% (Case Study G). While AI can personalize instructional con­
tent, it must also respond empathetically to learners’ emotional and motivational states. 
Systems that fail to detect disengagement or frustration may reduce the efficacy of per­
sonalization. Incorporating features like real-time emotional feedback, gamification, and 
interactive design can help sustain interest and deepen learning experiences [5, 11].
In conclusion, although AI holds significant promise for transforming digital educa­
tion, its deployment must be guided by a nuanced understanding of its inherent chal­
lenges. As consolidated in Table 8, addressing these trade-offs through careful design 
and governance is vital. Ensuring data privacy, algorithmic fairness, interpretability, 
accessibility, and learner engagement is essential for fostering responsible, human-cen­
tered AI systems in education [1, 2, 71].

One prominent development is the growing application of attention-based deep learn­

sequential learning behaviors and forecasting academic trajectories. By identifying key

sequencing tailored to individual learner needs [16, 41].
Another promising area is the advancement of multimodal and sensor-driven learning 
environments. These systems aggregate data from diverse sources including eye track­
ing, facial expression analysis, physiological signals, and behavioral logs to generate rich 
learner profiles. Integrating cognitive and affective information supports more empa­

The increasing demand for transparency in AI-driven decision-making has accelerated 
the development of XAI. These frameworks are designed to explain how models produce 
their outputs, allowing educators and other stakeholders to interpret and trust system-
generated recommendations. In education, where AI influences learning pathways and 
institutional accountability, ensuring explainability is essential for both adoption and 
legitimacy [7, 50].
Hybrid instructional models are also gaining traction, combining AI’s analytical capa­
bilities with the emotional intelligence and pedagogical judgment of human educators. 
In these models, AI supports functions such as learner diagnostics, content matching, 
and feedback generation, while educators focus on mentoring, motivation, and deeper 
cognitive engagement. Professional development programs that prepare teachers to 
interpret and apply AI insights will be crucial to the success of such approaches [2, 6].

9  Conclusion
This systematic review has examined the multifaceted role of artificial intelligence (AI) 
in advancing adaptive and personalized learning within digital education environments. 
The findings highlight the transformative potential of AI, particularly through machine 
learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning, in delivering instruction that 
responds to learners’ individual needs, preferences, and engagement patterns [1, 2].
AI technologies contribute significantly to the development of intelligent tutoring 
systems, real-time content adaptation, predictive learner modeling, and data-driven 
feedback mechanisms. Supervised and unsupervised learning approaches have proven 
effective in classifying learner behaviors and tailoring instructional strategies, while rein­
forcement learning supports the dynamic sequencing of content that enhances learner 
autonomy and performance [12, 16].
Although deep learning architectures offer robust capabilities for modeling complex, 
multimodal educational data, their broader implementation is constrained by technical 
barriers such as computational intensity, limited data availability, and low model inter­
pretability. Nonetheless, recent integrations particularly those involving deep reinforce­
ment learning and multimodal analytics demonstrate the emerging potential of these 
approaches to foster more responsive and empathetic learning environments [13, 41].
Despite these advancements, persistent challenges must be addressed to ensure ethical 
and equitable deployment of AI in education. Concerns around data privacy, algorith­
mic bias, infrastructural limitations, and cultural adaptability remain pressing. Future 
progress will depend on the adoption of explainable AI techniques, culturally respon­
sive design frameworks, and inclusive development practices that promote fairness and 
transparency [7, 50].
Looking ahead, the success of AI in education will hinge on sustained interdisciplin­
ary collaboration among educators, developers, researchers, and policymakers. To fully 
realize the benefits of AI-enhanced learning, it is essential to develop systems that are 
not only technically advanced and scalable, but also pedagogically grounded and socially 
inclusive. With thoughtful design, continuous innovation, and a commitment to equity, 
AI can support the creation of learning ecosystems that are more personalized, engag­
ing, and learner-centered [5, 71]. Moreover, this review provides a foundation for future 
research in the era of generative AI including large language models (LLMs), multimodal

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed digital education by enabling personalized and data-driven learning experiences. By incorporating machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and multimodal analytics, AI systems adapt instructional content to match individual learner profiles in real time. This systematic review examines AI-powered adaptive learning technologies with an emphasis on supervised and unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning (RL), and multimodal data integration. It assesses how these technologies enhance personalization, boost learner engagement, and promote educational equity. Adhering to PRISMA guidelines, this review analyzes 142 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025, sourced from databases including Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. Studies were selected based on their application of AI techniques in personalized digital learning environmen. Supervised learning models such as support vector machines (SVMs) and decision trees support learner classification and performance prediction. Unsupervised clustering techniques uncover behavioral patterns, while reinforcement learning enables dynamic content sequencing to foster learner autonomy. Multimodal approaches that integrate affective and biometric data further refine personalization. Despite these advances, critical challenges persist in model interpretability, data privacy, and scalability, especially in low-resource settings. This review highlights the expanding influence of AI in personalized education and outlines future research directions, including the use of explainable AI (XAI), modular system designs, and culturally responsive frameworks. These advancements are vital for developing ethical, inclusive, and scalable learning systems.
